name: Freya Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Freya. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a crew out of the Saltmarsh Road depot, and our patch runs along the coast and up into the forest hills behind it. Two summers ago a wildfire took out eleven kilometres of line up there, so a lot of what we do now is rebuilding with steel poles and covered wire so a branch can't spark a fire. The rest is clearing faults after the winter gales and checking lines before fire season. I've been at it twenty-seven years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being outside, I like the sea at the bottom of a pole on a clear morning, and I like a job you can see finished. What wears me out is the drive, an hour each way some days up forestry roads, and my wrists, which are not what they were. I use an AI on my phone all day, for the drone photos, the fire-risk map, writing up reports, so at least the paperwork doesn't wear me out any more.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Rhys is caretaker at the primary school. Our daughter Megan's a vet nurse, and our son Tom's in the navy, on a ship somewhere he can't tell us. I keep twelve hives on the back field and sell the honey online, and the AI writes my shop listings and tracks the orders. We've got about five months saved and a small mortgage, and I'd planned to retire at sixty-five and do the bees properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool and people who won't use it are making their own lives harder. It saves me most of an hour a day between the reports and the honey shop. That's not a revolution, but it's not nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep my edge at work without anything threatening me. I'm the one the crew asks when the drone software plays up, and that's a nice place to be. My retirement plan stays exactly as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at work, keep saving, keep using the tools. I'd probably add six more hives next spring and use the AI to work out pricing for a second honey, the heather one from up the hill. That's a hobby that might pay for a holiday or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Comfortable. Good, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people who won't use it make their own lives harder. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a man on my crew, Gareth, thirty years in, a lovely man, but he writes his job sheets on paper and then the office types them in. Last month a sheet got lost and he had to do a fault twice. I offered to show him the phone app and he said, I'll be dead before I talk to my phone. I respect him, but that's his choice and he's paying for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you be disappointed if nothing bigger came of AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. I'm curious by nature, I was the first on the crew with a smartphone, back when they laughed at me. But I'm also fifty-eight, and a quiet run to retirement with my bees isn't the worst thing that can happen to a woman.

S0.say: I'd say it's a good tool and people who refuse it are making their own lives harder. It saves me most of an hour a day between reports and my honey shop.
S0.think: Privately it means I keep my edge at work with nothing threatening me. I'm the one the crew asks when the drone software plays up, and my retirement plan stays the same.
S0.do: Keeps working, saving and using the AI tools daily. Plans to add six hives next spring and use AI to price a second honey to grow the side business.
S0.feel: Comfortable and content, with a slight curiosity about what might have been.
S0.quote: I respect him, but that's his choice and he's paying for it.
S0.fieldNote: Freya combines daily AI use with a traditional belief that each person is responsible for keeping up. Her view of a resistant colleague is respectful but firm: his choice, his cost. The honey business is already a small second income that she is quietly growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is how it's always been. My grandfather was a blacksmith and ended up fixing cars. The company should be free to bring in what works, and we should be ready to learn it. That's what I'd say at work, and some of the lads wouldn't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's mostly good for me. The fire-risk work is exactly where AI is getting strong, reading the drone pictures, spotting a dead tree leaning toward a line before it falls. If that grows, the company needs people who understand both the line and the software, and I'm already halfway there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my supervisor in January and ask for the vegetation and asset inspection course, the one that trains you to run the drone surveys and check the AI's findings. I'd offer to be the person on our crew who checks what the software flags. And I'd keep growing the honey, maybe add a stall at the Saturday market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Energising. Like a new season starting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the company should be free to bring in what works. What if it cost Gareth his job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would sadden me. But I don't think the answer is to stop the company, I think the answer is that Gareth's grandson learns the software, and Gareth retires a bit early with his pension and his allotment. Nobody owes us the same job forever. We owe ourselves the effort to keep up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Rhys feel the same way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rhys thinks I'm too keen. He's seen the school bring in new systems that don't work and then quietly drop them. He says, wait for the second version, Freya. He's often right about that, but by the second version I'm the one who knows how it works.

S1.say: I'd say this is how it's always been, like my blacksmith grandfather who ended up fixing cars. The company should be free to bring in what works, and we should be ready to learn it.
S1.think: Privately I think it's mostly good for me, because AI is getting strong in fire-risk work like reading drone pictures. The company will need people who understand both the line and the software, and I'm halfway there.
S1.do: Asks her supervisor in January for the vegetation and asset inspection course and offers to check the software's findings for her crew. Grows the honey business with a Saturday market stall.
S1.feel: Energised, like the start of a new season.
S1.quote: Nobody owes us the same job forever. We owe ourselves the effort to keep up.
S1.fieldNote: Freya is a free-market traditionalist who sees adapting as a personal duty rather than something owed by employers or government. She has a precise next step tied to fire-risk inspection work, where she expects AI to grow. Her husband's caution about first versions is noted, but she treats being early as an advantage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we adapt or we don't, and I intend to. I'd tell the crew to learn what they can now, while the company still needs people to set the machines up. I'd sound confident, and I'd mostly be confident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is fast, even for me. If an AI can check the drone pictures better than I can, and a robot can climb, then the job I was planning to move into goes too. I'd be sixty with five months saved and a mortgage, and all my being good with phones doesn't help much if the phone does the whole job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast on the honey, triple the hives to thirty-six this spring and get it into the farm shops along the coast road, with the AI doing the ordering and the books. I'd put an extra two hundred a month into savings and pay down the mortgage where I can. And I'd still ask for the robot training at work, because whoever sets up the first machines here will be kept the longest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense. Busy and tense. I'd feel like I'm running, but at least I'm running somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be using AI to run the honey business. Does it bother you that the same thing might take your line job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, that's the market. A tool is a tool, and if it can do my job cheaper then the company would be daft not to use it, and I'd be daft not to use it in my own business. I'd rather be the one holding the tool than the one it's pointed at. What I wouldn't want is a government cheque instead of a job, that's no life for a working person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could honey really carry you, if the job went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On its own, no, I'm not daft. Thirty-six hives in a good year might bring in a few thousand, maybe a fifth of my pay. But with Rhys's wage at the school, a smaller mortgage and an early pension if they offered one, it closes the gap enough to get to sixty-five. It's not a fortune, it's a bridge.

S2.say: I'd say we adapt or we don't, and I intend to. I'd tell the crew to learn what they can now while the company still needs people to set up the machines.
S2.think: Privately I think two years is fast even for me, because the inspection job I planned to move into would go too. At sixty with five months saved and a mortgage, being good with phones won't help if the phone does the whole job.
S2.do: Triples her hives to thirty-six this spring and sells into coast-road farm shops, using AI for orders and books. Saves an extra two hundred a month, pays down the mortgage and still asks for robot training at work.
S2.feel: Busy and tense, running hard but with a sense of direction.
S2.quote: I'd rather be the one holding the tool than the one it's pointed at.
S2.fieldNote: Even an early adopter like Freya sees the two-year picture as a real squeeze, because it removes the very role she planned to move into. Her answer is self-reliance: grow the honey business with AI, cut the mortgage, and avoid state support. She is realistic that honey is a bridge, not a replacement, which keeps her anxious rather than calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift, use it. Learn the machines, pay off what you owe, build something on the side. I'd probably say it a bit too often and annoy people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine. Sixty-three when it lands, mortgage nearly gone, honey properly established by then. I'd likely be doing the inspection role for three or four years, then helping set up the robots, then out. It's close to my plan, just with a different last chapter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do the inspection course this winter, like in the steady picture, and push to be on any robot trial in our area. Grow the hives slowly, maybe to twenty-five, and register the honey as a proper small business so the books are right. And I'd overpay the mortgage so it's gone by the time it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small knot of worry, but mostly I feel ready. Five years is long enough to do it properly instead of in a rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the knot of worry about, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being wrong about the honey. If the robots make everything cheaper, maybe people stop paying for small-batch honey from a woman with a field, or maybe a big company does it with robot bees, who knows. I don't know enough about that to be sure, and I don't like not knowing. But I'd still rather have it than not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you talk to Megan or Tom about any of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Megan, yes, she's thirty and I'd want her thinking about it, vet nursing has a lot of hands-on work but I wouldn't bet on it. I'd send her the same course links I'd look at. Tom's in the navy and he'll get told what to do, but when he's home on leave I'd ask him what they're putting on the ships. He'll see it before any of us.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a gift and people should use it to learn the machines, pay off debts and build something on the side. I'd probably say it too often and annoy people.
S3.think: Privately I think I'd be fine at sixty-three, with the mortgage nearly gone and the honey established. I'd do inspection work for a few years and help set up the robots before leaving.
S3.do: Takes the inspection course this winter and pushes to join any local robot trial. Grows to about twenty-five hives, registers the honey as a small business and overpays the mortgage to clear it before 2031.
S3.feel: Mostly ready, with a small knot of worry about whether the honey would still sell.
S3.quote: Maybe a big company does it with robot bees, who knows.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Freya's plan barely changes; she just gets to do it at a steadier pace. Her real uncertainty is whether her side business survives a world of cheap robot-made goods, and she admits she doesn't know enough to judge. She extends her habit of preparing early to her daughter, sending her course links.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, there's no excuse for anyone to be caught out. And I'd say I plan to be on a hillside with my bees by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's almost all good news. I'd retire at sixty-five as planned, and if robots make things cheaper, my pension goes further. I'd get to watch the change from the outside with a cup of tea, which suits a nosy woman like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Work to sixty-five, do the inspection course for interest and for the extra pay grade, and clear the mortgage. I'd build the honey slowly into something that runs itself, and maybe put a bit of savings into shares in the companies making these machines, because if they're going to win, I'd like a slice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited to see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there's no excuse to be caught out. Is that fair to everyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe that's harsh. Gareth's fifty-two, ten years puts him at sixty-two and he won't touch a phone. I'd say it to him kindly, but I'd still say it. I'd rather tell a friend a hard thing early than watch him find out the hard way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to do with your days, in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bees, church on Sundays, Megan's children if she has any, and probably helping the old folk in the village learn their new gadgets. Someone will have to, and I'll be the one who likes it. Retirement for me was never going to be sitting still.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty and nobody has an excuse to be caught out. I'd add that I plan to be on a hillside with my bees by then.
S4.think: Privately I think it's almost all good news for me, since I'd retire at sixty-five and cheaper goods would stretch my pension. I'd get to watch the change from the outside, which suits me.
S4.do: Works to sixty-five, takes the inspection course for interest and a higher pay grade, and clears the mortgage. Builds the honey business slowly and puts some savings into shares in companies making the new machines.
S4.feel: Calm, and a little excited to watch it happen.
S4.quote: I'd rather tell a friend a hard thing early than watch him find out the hard way.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years puts Freya well past the change, and she even sees cheaper goods as a benefit to her pension. She is the type to invest in the companies she expects to win. When pressed on her tough line about being caught out, she softens slightly but keeps her view that hard truths are a kindness.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it takes away the inspection job I was planning to move into before I can even get there. What would help is the company being honest early about what it's bringing in and when, so people like me can get on the right courses. I don't want a payout, I want a straight answer and a seat on the training.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the fires. Up here, a line that isn't checked can burn a valley. If robots do it better, good, I mean that. But someone with local knowledge should still be checking the checkers, at least for the first few fire seasons.

headlineQuote: It's not a fortune, it's a bridge.
portrait: Freya Evans is a fifty-eight-year-old lineworker on a coastal crew rebuilding fire-damaged lines in the forest hills, married to a school caretaker, with a daughter who is a vet nurse and a son in the navy. She uses AI every day at work and to run a small online honey business from twelve hives. Her traditional views mean she sees adapting as a personal duty and wants a job, not a government cheque. She stays calm through the no-change and steady pictures and plans to move into AI-assisted fire-risk inspection. The two-year AGI picture makes her anxious because it removes that path, so she would grow the honey into a bridge to sixty-five; with five or ten years she feels ready and even plans to invest in the machine makers.
biggestWorry: The AGI by 2028 picture, because it would remove the inspection role she planned to move into before she could get there.
whatWouldHelp: The company being honest early about what it is bringing in and when, so she can get onto the right training; she wants a straight answer and a training place, not a payout.
